title_eng: Feasibility Study of Sitting Posture Monitoring Based on Piezoresistive Conductive Film-Based Flexible Force Sensor
abstract:
IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 16, NO. 1, JANUARY 1, 2016 15
Feasibility Study of Sitting Posture Monitoring Based on Piezoresistive
Conductive Film-Based Flexible Force Sensor
Byung Woo Lee and Hangsik Shin, Member, IEEE
Abstract— A study was conducted to develop a force sensor
made of piezoresistive conductive ﬁlm and to assess the feasibility
of detecting inappropriate sitting postures using the force sensor
platform. The force sensor was designed with multiple layers
and includes a conductive foil and an insulation cover. The sensor
delivers voltage output according to its power-law characteristics
in response to a change in the applied force. The distribution
of pressure was measured for three postures—upright, forward
leaning, and backward leaning—using a three-by-three sensor
array attached to a chair. The results indicate that the ratio of
the average pressure distribution on the front row to that on the
rear row of the sensor array exhibits a signiﬁcant variation.
Index Terms — Biomedical monitoring, ergonomics, force
sensors, piezoelectric ﬁlms, sitting posture.
I. I NTRODUCTION
A
N INAPPROPRIATE sitting posture can give rise to
musculoskeletal diseases such as cervical disk and for-
ward head posture syndrome and lumbago [1]. Considerable
research has been conducted on detecting and correcting the
sitting posture, including detection of inappropriate postures
based on output from an accelerom eter [2], [3], inducement of
posture correction through analysis of the function and fatigue
of the muscles around the spine using electromyography [4],
identiﬁcation of correct posture with the help of images
captured using a camera [4], [5], and estimation of posture
through analysis of the distribution of pressure using pressure
sensors [6] or textile-based pressure sensor [7] mounted on a
chair. Posture analysis based on pressure sensors is useful to
because it can reveal the distribution and balance of load and
weight intuitively. The aims of this study were to develop a
novel force sensor using a type of piezoresistive polymer ﬁlm,
and to verify the feasibility of detecting inappropriate sitting
postures using the force sensor platform.

III. M EASUREMENT OF PRESSURE DISTRIBUTION DURING
VARIOUS POSTURES USING FORCE SENSOR PLATFORM
To conﬁrm the feasibility of measuring the force distribution
during various sitting postures, we developed a three-by-three
sensor array and attached it to a chair. Data were recorded from
every sensor simultaneously at a 100-Hz sampling frequency.
The forces were measured for three postures: upright (UP),
forward leaning (FL) and back ward leaning (BL). Seven
participants (two males and ﬁve females), 22 ± 0.58 years
in age, 168.9 ± 6.57 cm in height, and 59.14 ± 4.35 kg in
weight, participated in the experiment. The subjects voluntarily
and provided their consent to take part in the experiment.
In the experiment, the force distribution was measured for
each of the three postures for a period of 10 s, and this was
repeated ten times. Figure 3 shows the ratio of the average
pressure measured at the front row to that at the rear row
of the sensor array. The front–back ratio (F/B ratio), i.e., the
ratio of the average front-side voltage output to the average
back-side voltage output, was 0.605, 0.248, and 2.333 for the
UP, FL, and BL postures, respectively. These results indicate
that the pressure is concentrated in the middle part of the
thighs in the FL posture, whereas the pressure is concentrated
on the buttocks in the BL posture.
IV . DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
The results show that the proposed sensor can be used in
force sensing and that the proposed sensing platform based on
a sensor array can clearly discriminate between the BL and
other postures. However, the sensing platform might not be
able to distinguish between the UP and FL postures. This could
be a result of the experimental environment. For example, in
the FL posture, a participant leans on a table, and this could
reduce the pressure on the seat. The experimental environment
used in this study was designed to consider practical situations
such as those in the ofﬁce or classroom. To provide more
generalized results, a more controlled experiment environment
should be used in further research. The sensor can be man-
ufactured at approximately half the price of existing sensors
such as a load cell, a force-sensing resistor (FSR) [9], and
polyvinylidene ﬂuoride (PVDF) [10]. The competitive price
and ease of manufacture of the sensor make it possible for the
sensing area to be segmented into small pieces, which could
minimize a blind area of pressure measurement. Further study
is needed to increase the resolu tion by increasing the number
of sensors and the measurement area. Also, determining the
sensor size and position is needed to optimize the sensor
platform and permit quantiﬁcation of the measured results.
